adversePossession.value: 10 years (with color of title, taxes listed, or inheritance)
adversePossession.detail: Statutory adverse possession requires 10 years plus a recorded deed or color of title, 10 years of listing the land for taxes, or title by inheritance or devise.

squatterRemoval.detail: An owner can give law enforcement a sworn affidavit that the occupant is not a tenant, holdover tenant or family member; police then serve notice and remove the unauthorized person (Act 2024-237).

adversePossession.detail: An action to recover real property must be brought within 10 years, so 10 years of adverse possession can bar the owner's claim.

The owner must sue within 10 years against someone in peaceable and adverse possession who uses the property; shorter periods apply with color of title (3 years) or a recorded deed plus taxes (5 years).

squatterRemoval.detail: A 2026 law makes it a forcible detainer when an unauthorized occupant (not a tenant, cohabitant or family member) refuses a reasonable request to leave, so owners can file without the usual 5-day wait.

adversePossession.value: 7 years (with color of title and taxes paid)
adversePossession.detail: Suits to recover land must be brought within 7 years, and the claimant generally must also have paid property taxes for 7 years under color of title.

squatterRemoval.value: Police report for criminal squatting (Ark. Code § 5-39-215)
squatterRemoval.detail: Since 2025, unlawful squatting is a crime; an owner can report it to police, and an occupant who can't produce a deed, lease, written permission or recent rent receipt can be charged.

adversePossession.detail: The claimant must occupy the land continuously for 5 years and pay all property taxes levied during that time.

squatterRemoval.detail: California has no squatter-specific removal law; owners use a forcible entry/detainer (unlawful detainer) court action.

adversePossession.detail: Owners must sue within 18 years; a 7-year period applies with color of title plus tax payments, and claims must be proven by clear and convincing evidence.

squatterRemoval.detail: Owners use Colorado's forcible entry and detainer action, which covers anyone who enters without right or title.

adversePossession.detail: An owner must re-enter or act within 15 years after being ousted from possession.

squatterRemoval.detail: Owners use summary process (eviction) against someone who never had a right to occupy, after a notice to quit.

adversePossession.detail: No one may enter or sue to recover land more than 20 years after the right accrued.
Actions to recover land must be brought within 15 years.

squatterRemoval.detail: Owners file a forcible entry and detainer action in D.C. Superior Court against anyone holding property without right.

adversePossession.value: 7 years (with taxes paid or color of title)
adversePossession.detail: Florida requires 7 years of continuous possession, either under color of title or, without title, with all property taxes paid and a return filed with the property appraiser.

squatterRemoval.detail: An owner can give the sheriff a sworn complaint; if the occupant is not a tenant or family member, the sheriff serves a notice to vacate immediately and restores possession.

adversePossession.detail: Possession meeting the statutory requirements for 20 years gives title by prescription; 7 years suffices under written color of title.

squatterRemoval.detail: Unlawful squatting is a crime; the accused gets a citation and must show a lease or other authorization within 3 business days or face arrest, with a fast magistrate-court affidavit process.

adversePossession.detail: Actions to recover land must be brought within 20 years, and a claimant must also show good faith to establish title by adverse possession.

squatterRemoval.detail: Hawaii has no squatter-specific removal law; owners use a summary possession or ejectment action in court.

adversePossession.detail: The land must be occupied and claimed continuously for 20 years with all taxes paid, proven by clear and convincing evidence.

squatterRemoval.detail: An owner can ask the county sheriff for immediate removal of people unlawfully occupying residential property if listed conditions are met (2025 law).

adversePossession.detail: Actions to recover land must be brought within 20 years; a 7-year period applies to possession under record title from certain sources (such as tax or court sales).

squatterRemoval.value: Police removal for criminal trespass (735 ILCS 5/9-102(e))
squatterRemoval.detail: Since Jan. 1, 2026, eviction law does not stop police from enforcing criminal trespass and removing squatters; otherwise owners file an eviction.

adversePossession.detail: Actions to recover possession of real estate must be brought within 10 years, and an adverse possessor must pay the taxes they reasonably believe are due.

squatterRemoval.value: Police removal by affidavit within 48 hours (SEA 157, 2025)
squatterRemoval.detail: An owner can sign an affidavit that a squatter (someone who never had a lease, permission or legal interest) is on the property; police must remove them within 48 hours unless there is credible evidence otherwise.

adversePossession.detail: Actions to recover real property must be brought within 10 years.

squatterRemoval.detail: Owners use Iowa's summary forcible entry and detainer action against someone who entered by force, fraud or stealth.

adversePossession.detail: Open, exclusive and continuous possession for 15 years, under a knowingly adverse claim or a belief of ownership, bars recovery.

squatterRemoval.value: Police removal by affidavit (Removal of Squatters Act)
squatterRemoval.detail: A 2026 law lets an owner submit a notarized affidavit to law enforcement to remove an unauthorized person from a dwelling unit.
squatterRemoval.cite: Kan. HB 2378 (2026), Removal of Squatters Act

adversePossession.detail: An action to recover real property must be brought within 15 years after the right accrued.

squatterRemoval.detail: An owner can present a petition to law enforcement to immediately remove someone who was never a tenant and has no agreement to occupy.

adversePossession.value: 30 years (10 with good faith and just title)
adversePossession.detail: Louisiana uses acquisitive prescription: 30 years of possession without title or good faith, or 10 years in good faith under just title.

squatterRemoval.value: Criminal trespass after demand; court injunction
squatterRemoval.detail: A squatter who fails to leave when told by the lawful possessor commits criminal trespass, and owners can get injunctive relief (Act 652 of 2024).

adversePossession.detail: Actions to recover land must be brought within 20 years after the right accrued.

squatterRemoval.detail: Owners use forcible entry and detainer, which can be brought against a disseisor (someone wrongfully in possession).

adversePossession.detail: An action to recover possession of land must be filed within 20 years.

squatterRemoval.detail: Owners file a wrongful detainer complaint in District Court; a 2025 law requires a hearing within 10 business days.

adversePossession.detail: An action to recover land must be brought within 20 years after the right accrued.

squatterRemoval.detail: Owners use summary process against a person who made a forcible entry or unlawfully holds possession.

adversePossession.detail: The general limitation period for actions to recover land is 15 years (shorter for certain tax and court-sale titles).

squatterRemoval.detail: Owners use summary proceedings to recover possession from someone who came in by trespass without color of title.

adversePossession.detail: Actions to recover real estate must be brought within 15 years; for separately assessed parcels the claimant must also have paid taxes for at least 5 consecutive years.

squatterRemoval.detail: Owners file an eviction action against a person who unlawfully or forcibly occupied the property.

adversePossession.detail: Ten years of actual adverse possession under a claim of ownership vests full title in the occupant.

squatterRemoval.value: Police citation by affidavit, then removal (HB 1200, 2025)
squatterRemoval.detail: An owner files a sworn affidavit with police, who cite the alleged squatter within 24 hours; the occupant must leave or ask the court for a hearing within 3 days, or be removed.
squatterRemoval.cite: Miss. HB 1200 (2025), Real Property Owners Protection Act

adversePossession.detail: An owner cannot recover land unless they possessed it within 10 years before suing.

squatterRemoval.value: Expedited court petition with ex parte order (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 534.602)
squatterRemoval.detail: Owners can file a verified petition to remove unlawful occupants of a residential dwelling; courts may issue an ex parte order enforced by the sheriff.

adversePossession.detail: Adverse possession requires 5 years of continuous occupation plus payment of all taxes levied on the land.

squatterRemoval.value: Police removal on request (Mont. Code Ann. § 70-24-113)
squatterRemoval.detail: A person who can't produce authorization to occupy may be removed immediately by law enforcement at the owner's request; squatting is also a crime (MCA 45-6-206).

adversePossession.detail: An action to recover title or possession of land must be brought within 10 years.

squatterRemoval.detail: Owners use a forcible entry and detainer action in county or district court.

adversePossession.detail: The land must be occupied and claimed for 5 continuous years with all taxes paid.

squatterRemoval.detail: After a notice to surrender, an unlawful occupant has 4 judicial days to contest; the court can order the sheriff or constable to remove them within 24 hours.

adversePossession.detail: No action to recover real estate may be brought after 20 years.

squatterRemoval.detail: Owners bring a possessory action against an occupant holding without right after written notice to quit.

adversePossession.detail: Thirty years of uninterrupted possession vests title (60 years for woodlands or uncultivated land).

squatterRemoval.detail: Entry into an occupied residence is allowed only through legal process, so owners must use a court action.

adversePossession.value: 10 years (with color of title, good faith and taxes paid)
adversePossession.detail: Title requires 10 years of continuous, good-faith adverse possession under color of title, with all taxes paid.
An adverse possessor gains title when the 10-year limit to recover real property expires, if possession was adverse, under claim of right, open, continuous, exclusive and actual.

squatterRemoval.detail: Since 2024, a squatter (someone who entered without permission and stays without title or right) is not a tenant, so tenant eviction protections don't apply.

adversePossession.detail: Twenty years of possession under known and visible boundaries gives title; 7 years suffices under color of title.

squatterRemoval.detail: A 2025 law creates an expedited court proceeding to remove unauthorized persons from residential property.

adversePossession.detail: An owner cannot recover real property unless they possessed it within 20 years before suing.

squatterRemoval.value: Felony trespass; police or court eviction
squatterRemoval.detail: Unlawfully occupying a residential dwelling is a class C felony (2025), so police can act; civil removal otherwise uses eviction.

adversePossession.detail: An action to recover title to or possession of real property must be brought within 21 years.

squatterRemoval.detail: Owners use forcible entry and detainer, which covers occupiers without color of title.

adversePossession.detail: Actions to recover real property not otherwise covered must be brought within 15 years.

squatterRemoval.value: Sheriff removal by complaint (21 Okla. Stat. § 1354)
squatterRemoval.detail: An owner can submit a verified complaint asking the sheriff to immediately remove unauthorized occupants who are not tenants or family members.

adversePossession.detail: Requires 10 years of actual, open, notorious, exclusive, hostile and continuous possession plus an honest, reasonable belief of ownership when possession began, proven by clear and convincing evidence.

squatterRemoval.value: Court eviction after 24-hour notice (2025 Or. Laws ch. 356)
squatterRemoval.detail: Owners may give a squatter 24 hours' written notice and then file an eviction (FED) action.

adversePossession.detail: Actions for possession of real property must be brought within 21 years; a 10-year period applies to small (half-acre or less) residential lots.
Ten years of uninterrupted, peaceful and actual possession under a claim of right gives title.
The owner is presumed in possession unless the land was held adversely for 10 years before the action.

squatterRemoval.detail: Since June 30, 2026, owners can file a verified petition with the clerk or chief magistrate to eject unlawful occupants of a residential dwelling, including ex parte orders.

adversePossession.value: 20 years (10 with color of title and taxes paid)
adversePossession.detail: An owner cannot recover land unless they possessed it within 20 years; 10 years of possession under color of title with taxes paid also vests title.

squatterRemoval.detail: Owners use forcible entry and detainer against someone who entered by force, fraud or stealth.

adversePossession.detail: Seven years of adverse possession under a recorded deed or other assurance of title vests title; suits to recover land are also barred after 7 years.

squatterRemoval.value: Sheriff removal by complaint (2024 Pub. Ch. 1009)
squatterRemoval.detail: An owner can ask the county sheriff for immediate removal of unlawful occupants of residential property if listed conditions are met (effective July 1, 2024).

adversePossession.detail: An owner must sue within 10 years against someone in peaceable and adverse possession who cultivates, uses or enjoys the property.

squatterRemoval.value: Sheriff/constable removal by complaint (Tex. Prop. Code ch. 24B)
squatterRemoval.detail: Since Sept. 1, 2025, an owner can file a sworn complaint asking the sheriff or constable to remove someone who unlawfully entered a dwelling and is not a tenant or family member.

adversePossession.detail: Adverse possession requires 7 years of continuous occupation and claim, with all taxes paid.

squatterRemoval.value: Police removal by verified complaint (Utah Code § 78B-6-817)
squatterRemoval.detail: An owner can present a verified complaint asking law enforcement to immediately remove a trespasser who is not a tenant or family member.

adversePossession.detail: An action to recover land must be brought within 15 years after it accrues.

squatterRemoval.detail: Owners bring an ejectment action to recover possession.

adversePossession.detail: No one may enter or sue to recover land more than 15 years after the right accrued.

squatterRemoval.detail: Owners file an unlawful entry or detainer action in court.

adversePossession.value: 10 years (7 with color of title and taxes paid)
adversePossession.detail: Actions to recover real property must be brought within 10 years; 7 years suffices with good-faith color of title and tax payments.

squatterRemoval.detail: Someone who enters without the owner's permission or color of title and won't leave after 3 days' notice is guilty of unlawful detainer and can be removed through court.

adversePossession.detail: No one may enter or sue to recover land more than 10 years after the right accrued.

squatterRemoval.value: Police removal by complaint (W. Va. Code § 55-3C-3)
squatterRemoval.detail: An owner can submit a verified complaint asking law enforcement to immediately remove a squatter from a residential or commercial building.

adversePossession.detail: An action to recover title or possession of land can only be brought within 10 years.

squatterRemoval.detail: Since July 1, 2025, an owner can ask law enforcement to immediately remove a person unlawfully occupying a residential dwelling who is not a tenant.
